lines: Election Day so far: registered Republicans 49.9% of voters, Democrats 25.9%, others 24.1%.
Florida's whole Election Day, Republicans and Democrats: 42.9% and 33.8% in 2018, 50.4% and 26.7% in 2022, 42.2% and 27.2% in 2024.
So far today looks like 2022's Election Day.

Every vote so far, mail, early and today: Republicans 42.5%, Democrats 34.9%. 2018 final: 42.6% and 37.3%. 2022 final: 45.5% and 33.4%. 2024 final: 42.7% and 31.7%. Today's votes are still coming in, so this mix moves toward the Election Day mix until the polls close.
Party is registration, not the vote. Who votes on the day also depends on how many voted early or by mail.

method: Every vote so far (mail, early and today) is R+7.6 by registration: Republicans minus Democrats. If Election Day ends as big as 2022's, the electorate lands near R+9.3. The final gap was R+5.3 in 2018, R+12.1 in 2022, R+11.1 in 2024.

How far each Senate result ran from that gap, which is how independents and crossover voters broke: 5.2 points bluer in 2018, 4.3 points redder in 2022, 1.7 points redder in 2024. The same this year gives R+4.1 to R+13.6.
means.ours_source: data/daily/2026-11-01.json core[senate_fl].margin (the core model on the closing day)
lines: Florida's turnout so far points to a Moody win in the Senate race, by somewhere around 4 to 14 points.
We forecast Moody by 5.6, near the Democratic end of that.

For our number to be right, independents and crossover voters have to lean Democratic this time, about as much as in 2018. If they vote like they did in 2022 and 2024, Moody wins by 11 or more, about 5 points redder than we expect.
What to watch tonight: Florida's count landing near Moody by 6 means our forecast is holding. Moody by 11 or more means the night is running redder than we expected.
Based on three past elections, and registration is not how people vote. A lean, not a call. It firms up as Election Day votes come in.
means.label: inferred
means.how: Registration gap = GOP share minus DEM share of the people voting. The range adds each year's gap between the Senate result and the registration gap to this year's projected gap. Scripts do the arithmetic (scripts/night_batches.py reading).

compare.label: inferred
compare.how: Shares of the people voting, by registration. 'Looks like' a year means the GOP-minus-DEM share gap is within 2 points of that year's whole Election Day.

lines: Early votes so far: 56.0 million in the 47 states we track, 53% of all the votes those states cast in 2022. In 21 states early votes already passed half of 2022's total. Where we can compare with the same point in 2022, turnout is ahead in 4 of 5.
Which way: only 4 states let us compare party with the same point in 2022. Mixed: North Carolina and Colorado bluer (5.2 and 3.5 points), Pennsylvania and Iowa redder (8.5 and 6.9 points).

What it means: our forecast has the country about 10 points bluer than 2022. The early vote shows a smaller shift than our forecast expects. But more Republicans vote early now than in 2022, so a redder early vote is not the same as a redder result. It says little about the final margin either way.

early_vote.how: Early votes against each state's total 2022 votes. The party comparison is the Democratic minus Republican share of early voters now against the same day before the 2022 election (data/dashboard/ev_swing.json).

how: Each report is the running count of today's voters by registration. A batch is the change from the report before. Scripts do the arithmetic (scripts/night_batches.py).
